turn_text: One thing I wanted to get back to which I was really interested in was how insurance companies and PBMs operate. So the insurance companies actually own the PBMs and sometimes it's vice versa. Sometimes you have a chain owning a PBM and an insurance company like in CBS's case, and the term that's used for this allows vertical integration. Is there something being done about vertical integration? Because that seems to be like the biggest crux of the problem. That these companies vertically integrated. There's no competition in this space. And as a result, they have this monopolistic control over drug pricing. Is there something in this package that may assist with that, do you think? In

this package, no. This package is the first step that takes on transparency, the really egregious incentive to increase the price of drugs and Medicare to get paid more. So it's an important first step. It does not take on the vertical integration challenge. Now, I have a bill, bipartisan and bicameral, that does take that next step. It's called the PBM Act, Patients' Before Monopolies Act. And that would require that PBM's cannot own pharmacies. Because going back to specialty steering, the misalignment of incentives is so profound there that it just should not be allowed to happen. In the same way that in the banking industry, after the Great Depression Congress said, listen, you can do kind of deposit and commercial banking, or you can do investment banking and speculation, but you can't do both. Because when you're using depositors' money to go out there and make wild speculative bets, The incentives just get too tangled up and we get bad behavior. It's not so dissimilar in the pharmaceutical supply chain where we basically say, you can be a formulary manager and provide that basic technical service of just developing formularies and managing data and managing reimbursements and claims, or you can own pharmacies and try to dispense and be a medical provider to patients. But you're not doing both because then you don't put the best interest of patients first. And so splitting those up is the next step. That's got bipartisan bicameral co-sponsorship. the align with it is another bill that I have called the pharmacist fight back act and this bill really drives to the interests of community and independent pharmacists because what it does is it establishes a system where pharmacists are getting paid a fair amount of money every time they dispense a drug, regardless of how much that drug costs. We've got to get out of this place where independent pharmacists get paid more or less depending on the price of the drug. We want to pay them because they are medical providers and they deserve to be compensated for the medical advice and service they are providing to their patients. And my bill drives us towards that outcome in a variety of ways.
